in Finland, economic and social attitudes are correlated, and this is driven by the fact that those on the left tend to be socially liberal, while those on the right tend to be socially conservative.

in a sample of Finnish municipal election candidates, the left-right and the liberal-conservative dimensions of political attitudes were moderately aligned, and that this alignment was driven by the left and the liberals being more egalitarian.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the relation between the economic and social dimensions of political attitudes, and with the psychological motivations underlying these dimensions.
the psychological underpinning of political attitudes in the political elite and the relation between these attitudes.
the relation between economic attitudes, social attitudes, and the psychological underpinning of these attitudes in a politically elite sample, and how these relations can be explained.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the left-right and the liberal-conservative dimensions of the political spectrum are not completely separate, but that they are more aligned among certain parts and less aligned among others.
the left-right and the liberal-conservative dimensions of political attitudes are moderately aligned among a certain part of the Finnish political elite.

social attitudes are more strongly associated with psychological motivations than economic ones, and that economic attitudes are associated with psychological motivations, but less consistently than social ones.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the left-right and conservative-liberal dimensions are moderately aligned in the political elite in Finland, and that the psychological underpinned of these attitudes are in line with what is expected by dual process models of ideology.
we have demonstrated that the psychological underpings of economic and social attitudes are not the same.
the political attitudes and psychological underpinnnings of the Finnish political elite are not as different as we might think.
The main takeaway from our work is that

even though economic and social attitudes are not necessarily correlated among the masses, they are correlated among the political elite, suggesting that political elites may be more likely to be motivated by the same psychological processes when making political decisions.

even in a political elite sample, the left-right and conservative-liberal dimensions are only moderately related, and that the relation between the dimensions is driven by underlying psychological motivations.

the left-right and social liberal-conservative dimensions can be traced to different underlying psychological motivations, and that these motivations are differentially associated with economic and social attitudes.
